turns.text: I'm autistic and I find eye contact and small talk in interviews really draining. Can I ask for changes?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, you can ask for reasonable adjustments. Many employers are used to it and will happily help.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What kind of adjustments are normal?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Getting the questions in writing beforehand, a quiet waiting area, or knowing exactly who'll be in the room. Some people ask for a little extra time to answer.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I have to say why?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can share as much or as little as you like. Saying it helps you give your best answers is often enough.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And eye contact during the interview itself?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Looking at the interviewer's forehead or the bridge of their nose looks natural to them and is often easier.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Every interview asks where do you see yourself in five years and I just have no idea.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's fine, they don't need a master plan. They mostly want to know you'll grow and stick around for a while.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I can just make something up?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Better to say something honest but general. For example, I'd like to be really skilled at this work and maybe leading small projects.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if I actually want to change careers eventually?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Leave that out. Focus on the next few years in this kind of role.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. So / honest, but not every detail.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. Honest, focused, and tied to what this job can offer you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have a phone screening tomorrow. Is it different from a normal interview?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's usually shorter and more about checking the basics, like your experience, availability and salary range.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I have notes in front of me?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, that's one of the perks. Just don't read them out word for word, it's easy to hear.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I stand or sit?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some people find standing makes their voice more energetic. Smiling while you talk also comes through in your tone.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I always feel weird talking to a stranger / with no face to look at.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Find a quiet spot and imagine you're chatting to a friendly colleague. It's a conversation, not an exam.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They offered me the job! But the salary is a bit lower than I hoped. Can I negotiate?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Congratulations! And yes, negotiating a fair offer is normal. How far off is it?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: About three thousand less than what I asked for.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a reasonable gap to try closing. Thank them warmly, then say you're excited but were hoping for a figure closer to your original number.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if they say no?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then ask about other things, like an earlier pay review, extra holiday, or a training budget.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm scared they'll take back the offer.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's very rare when you're polite and reasonable. Companies expect some negotiation.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm seventeen, going for a Christmas job at a toy shop. What will they ask?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Probably simple things. When you're free, why you want to work there, and how you'd handle a busy shop.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What do I say for why I want to work there? Money?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Money's honest, but add something else. Maybe that you like helping people or that you know lots about games and toys.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I do know a lot about board games.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect, mention that. Shops love staff who can actually recommend things.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if they ask about / a time I worked in a team? I've never had a job.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Use school or a club. A group project or a sports team counts. Just say what you did and how it turned out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I research a company before an interview? I usually just skim the homepage.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Go a bit deeper. Read their about page, a couple of recent news articles, and look at what they post on social media.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's a lot of reading.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Half an hour is plenty. You're looking for two or three things you can mention naturally.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like what kind of things?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A recent project, a value they talk about, or a new product. Then link it to yourself, like, I saw you launched this, and I'd love to work on something similar.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And should I look up / the person interviewing me too?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A quick look at their professional profile is fine. Just don't bring up anything personal.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm a chef and they want me to do a trial shift instead of a normal interview. What should I expect?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually a few hours in the kitchen, working a section or cooking a dish for the head chef. They're watching how you work as much as the food.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How I work, like speed?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Speed, cleanliness, how you take instructions, and how you get on with the team under pressure.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I bring my own knives?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, and your whites if you have them. Ask beforehand, but most chefs expect you to bring your own kit.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I always get flustered / when the head chef shouts.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Stay calm, say yes chef, and keep going. They're often testing how you handle that more than anything.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I spent twelve years in the army and civilian employers don't seem to get what I did.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a common challenge. The trick is translating military language into everyday business terms.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like what? I was a logistics sergeant.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Instead of rank, talk about responsibilities. For example, I managed a team of fifteen and moved equipment worth millions across three countries.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds way more impressive.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is impressive. You just need to say it in their language. Leadership, planning, working under pressure, these are all huge.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about the jargon / I use without even noticing?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ask a civilian friend to listen to your answers and stop you every time they don't understand a word.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, confession. I said on my CV that I'm advanced in spreadsheets and I'm really not.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Okay, honest question. How long until the interview?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Two weeks.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you have two options. Learn enough to be genuinely solid in that time, or be honest in the interview and say intermediate.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I actually learn that much in two weeks?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can get far. Focus on formulas, sorting and filtering, and basic charts. There are free tutorials for all of that.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if they test me / on something I don't know?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then admit it and explain how you'd find out. Pretending usually falls apart, but honesty plus curiosity tends to land well.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm four months pregnant and I've got an interview next week. Do I have to tell them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No, you're not legally required to tell them in many countries, and they shouldn't ask. It's your choice.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: But won't it feel sneaky if I get the job?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not at all. Lots of people choose to mention it after an offer, when it's about planning, not hiring.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I start showing by then?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it's up to you whether you say anything. Focus on your skills, that's what the interview is for.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I just don't want it / to count against me.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's understandable. If it ever seemed to affect their decision, that would be discrimination, and you'd have the right to challenge it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The interviewer was so rude. Checked his phone constantly and cut me off. And now they've offered me the job.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Mixed signals. Would he be your direct manager?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yes, unfortunately.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it's worth thinking about seriously. One bad day can happen, but how someone treats candidates often shows how they treat their team.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I find out if he's always like that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ask if you can talk to someone on the team before accepting. A quick chat with a future colleague tells you a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is that a normal thing to ask?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Totally normal, especially after an offer. If they say no, that's information too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friend says I look bored in interviews. I'm not, it's just my face.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha, resting serious face. Body language can fix a lot of that.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like what? I can't just grin the whole time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No, but lean forward slightly when they talk, nod now and then, and smile when you greet them and when you're talking about something you enjoy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I also tend to cross my arms.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try resting your hands loosely on the table instead. It looks more open and you'll feel less stiff.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Feels weird / but okay, I'll try it in the mirror.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Even better, record yourself answering a question on your phone. You'll see straight away what your friend means.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can you do a quick mock interview with me? Just one question.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sure. Tell me about a time you made a mistake at work, and what you did about it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Um, okay. Once I sent an invoice to the wrong client, and / I didn't notice until they emailed me.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Go on, what happened next?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I apologised, sent the right one, and set up a checklist so it wouldn't happen again.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a solid answer. The checklist is the best part, so say it with a bit more confidence.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I say how the client reacted?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, if it ended well. Something like, they appreciated the quick fix, rounds it off nicely.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friend's company is hiring and she offered to set up a coffee with her boss. Is that an interview or not?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's informal, but treat it as a gentle interview. First impressions still count.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I should dress up?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Smart casual is right. Not a suit, but something neat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And what do we even talk about?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ask about their work and what the team needs. Mention your background briefly, but let it feel like a conversation.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I ask about the job / directly, or is that too forward?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can, near the end. Something like, I'd love to hear more about the role your team is hiring for.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have a job talk for a lecturer post. Forty minutes to the whole department. I'm terrified.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a big one. Is it a talk about your research or a teaching demo?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Research, and then questions.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then keep it clear for people outside your exact field. Start with why the question matters, then your findings, then where you'd take it next.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My PhD supervisor says I go too deep into methods.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Listen to that. Give methods just enough to be trusted, and save the details for questions.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And when someone asks a hostile question?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Thank them, take a breath, and answer the part you can. It's fine to say, that's a great point, I'd want to look into it further.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm retired and I've applied to volunteer as a guide at the local history museum. Is there really an interview?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Often there is, though it's usually relaxed. They want to know you're reliable and enjoy talking to visitors.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I do love talking. My wife says too much.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's actually useful for a guide. Just show you can also listen and adjust to who's in front of you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like children, you mean?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. A school group needs something different from a group of local historians.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I suppose I could / tell them about the tours I used to give at the church.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's perfect. It shows you've done something similar and enjoyed it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Consulting firm. Case interview. I have no idea what that is.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They give you a business problem, like why a company's profits are falling, and you work through it out loud with them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: With no data?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They'll give you some as you ask. The point is to structure the problem, ask good questions, and do some quick maths.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maths in my head. Brilliant.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's usually simple percentages and multiplication. Practise doing it out loud and round numbers to keep it easy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Any books or anything?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: There are popular case prep books and plenty of free practice cases online. Doing a few with a friend is the best preparation.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's midnight, my interview is at ten, and I can't sleep.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's so normal the night before. Have you prepared what you can?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yes. I've gone over everything like twenty times.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then the preparation is done. Going over it again now will just keep your brain buzzing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: But what if I forget everything tomorrow?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You won't. Preparation sticks. Try writing down any worries on a piece of paper, then put it away.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if I still / can't fall asleep?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Just rest with your eyes closed. Even a quiet, lying down rest helps, and nerves will give you energy in the morning.

option_sets.lead_in: I've got a job interview on Thursday and I'm trying to decide how to prepare.
options: The first option is writing out answers to common questions and memorizing them.
Then there's doing a practice interview with my friend who works in hiring.
And the last one is spending the time researching the company and their recent projects.
moshi_comment: The practice interview with your friend is probably the most valuable, since you'll get real feedback. Researching the company is important too, it helps you ask good questions. Memorizing answers word for word can make you sound stiff.
Is this a company you know a lot about already? If not, spend an evening on research, then do the practice interview. Just jot down key points for common questions instead of memorizing full answers.

option_sets.lead_in: I got two job offers and a maybe on a third, and I need help thinking it through.
options: The first one pays the most, but it's an hour commute each way and the team seemed kind of tense.
Then there's a smaller company, a bit less money, but fully remote with a really friendly manager.
Option three is a big company with great benefits and training, but the role is pretty junior.
And the last one is the maybe, a startup doing something exciting, but they haven't made an offer yet.
moshi_comment: The remote job with the friendly manager sounds really appealing, a good boss makes a huge difference day to day. The highest paying job might not be worth two hours of commuting and a tense team. The big company is a solid choice if you want training and stability.

What matters most to you right now, money, growth, or quality of life? If it's quality of life, the remote job is the clear pick. I wouldn't wait too long on the startup, since they haven't even made an offer.

option_sets.lead_in: I found three job postings I like and I can only realistically prepare properly for one this week.
options: A marketing coordinator role at a small charity, lower pay but a mission I really care about.
A junior brand manager job at a big drinks company, great salary and a long hiring process.
Or a social media role at an agency, fast paced, and they want someone to start right away.
moshi_comment: The charity role matches your values, and small teams often hire faster. The drinks company pays best, but a long process means you can apply now and prepare later. The agency is the quickest route to a job, though fast paced can mean burnout.

If you need income soon, the agency makes sense to prepare for first. If you can wait, the charity is the one you sound most excited about. I'd send the drinks company application now anyway, since that process will take weeks.

option_sets.lead_in: They'll ask me about a time I handled a challenge, and I've got a few stories but can't pick.
options: There's when our main supplier went bust and I found a new one in three days.
Another is when I had to calm down a really angry customer who was shouting in the shop.
There's also the time I trained two new starters while my manager was off sick for a month.
Or when I caught a big billing mistake that would have cost us thousands.
moshi_comment: The supplier story shows you act fast under pressure, which is great for an operations role. The angry customer is more about patience and people skills. Training the new starters shows leadership, and the billing catch shows attention to detail.

Pick based on the job. For a team lead role, the month of training new starters is strongest. For anything with numbers, the billing mistake. Keep the angry customer as a backup for a question about difficult people.

option_sets.lead_in: I need to present one piece from my design portfolio in the interview and I'm stuck.
options: A rebrand for a local bakery, which is my prettiest work, but the brief was pretty simple.
An app redesign for a bus company, less pretty, but I ran real user tests and it improved bookings.
Or a poster series for a music festival, really bold and fun, done as a personal project.
moshi_comment: The bus app is your strongest story, because you can show a problem, testing, and a measurable result. The bakery looks lovely but there's less to talk about. The festival posters show personality, and might be good to mention briefly at the end.

Interviewers usually care more about your process than polish, so the bus company redesign wins. Keep the bakery images ready if they want to see visual style. The posters are a nice extra if they ask what you do for fun.

option_sets.lead_in: I've got to give them two references, and I'm not sure which people to pick.
options: My old team leader from the warehouse, who loved me but that was five years ago.
My current manager, who's fine, but I haven't told her I'm looking yet.
A client I worked closely with for two years who always says I'm brilliant.
Or my college tutor, who knows me well but only from studying.
moshi_comment: The client sounds like a strong, recent reference who's seen your work directly. The warehouse team leader is enthusiastic but a bit dated. Your current manager is ideal eventually, but only once you're ready to tell her.

I'd go with the client and the old team leader for now. Ask the company to contact your current manager only after an offer, that's a very normal request. Your tutor is better for a first job than for this one.
